title: Who's really behind the screen?
preparation: Open the PDF (or the SlideForge deck) on the board before the class arrives.
This topic can be distressing for students who have experienced image-based abuse: have your safeguarding lead's name ready to say, and details to share privately.
Optional: be ready to show a reverse image search (Google Lens or TinEye).

instructions.action: Have the title up as the class comes in.
instructions.teacher_tip: Frame it sensitively — some students may have personal experience of this.

instructions.action: Ask the question and give pairs 60 seconds. Take a vote on the four options by hands or phones.
instructions.teacher_tip: "Send it to a friend to check" is the teachable answer: it feels responsible and it is the one that spreads the harm. Do not say so until after the vote.

instructions.action: Read the headline aloud and let the room work out what "1 in 17" means for a class of thirty.
instructions.teacher_tip: Pause after "1 in 17" and say that support is always available. State 98% once and move on.

instructions.action: Take the room's answers first, then go through the four cards, matching them to what was said.
instructions.teacher_tip: Say plainly that forwarding something to warn people is still forwarding it, and that creating AI-generated intimate images of anyone is illegal.

instructions.action: Turn the lesson back on the deck: go through the source check row by row.
instructions.teacher_tip: Be fair to the number — it is a serious figure from a serious source. The point is that nobody asked.

instructions.action: Leave the two definitions up for pupils to copy.
Go through the three habits.
instructions.teacher_tip: If you are short of time, end here.

instructions.action: Read the takeaway, then stop talking.
Say, out loud, who pupils can go to if anything today affected them, and leave the support slides up as the room moves on.
instructions.teacher_tip: Name the actual person — tutor, head of year or safeguarding lead — rather than leaving it to the slide.

title: How does AI actually 'think'?
preparation: Open the PDF (or the SlideForge deck) on the board before the class arrives.
Optional: have ChatGPT or a similar tool ready to show one answer live.

instructions.action: Have the title up as the class comes in.
instructions.teacher_tip: Frame it as curious exploration: how does a tool they already use actually work?

instructions.action: Ask the question, give pairs 60 seconds, then take the vote.
instructions.teacher_tip: Note who says AI "thinks" for gentle correction later. "Somewhere in between" is the most interesting answer to unpick.

instructions.action: Walk through the four rows: what a language model does, against what understanding would need.
instructions.teacher_tip: This slide is the whole starter. If you only have two minutes, show the question and then this.

instructions.action: Read the three figures: nearly everyone uses it, and half already know it makes things up.
instructions.teacher_tip: A hallucination is not a rare glitch. It is what prediction does when the pattern runs out.

instructions.action: Go through the four answer cards, matching them to what pairs said.
instructions.teacher_tip: Do not skip the last card: explaining the limits should not tip into "AI is rubbish".

instructions.action: Leave the two definitions up for pupils to copy.
Go through the three habits and invite pupils to name one they will change.
instructions.teacher_tip: Emphasise "Verify". If you are short of time, end here.

instructions.action: Read the takeaway, then stop.
Say, out loud, who pupils can go to if anything today affected them, and leave the support slides up as the room moves on.
instructions.teacher_tip: Name the actual person — tutor, head of year or safeguarding lead — rather than leaving it to the slide.

title: AI as your creative partner
preparation: Open the PDF (or the SlideForge deck) on the board before the class arrives.
Optional: have one example of a student creative task to refer to when discussing AI's role.

instructions.action: Have the title up and introduce AI as a creative partner, not a replacement.
instructions.teacher_tip: Frame it positively: this is about enhancing creativity, not threatening it.

instructions.action: Ask the question, give pairs 60 seconds, then take the vote.
instructions.teacher_tip: Accept a range of answers and let two people who voted differently argue it out. Do not resolve it.

instructions.action: Read the three figures aloud.
instructions.teacher_tip: The "None" tile often surprises students — let it land, and take the pushback.

instructions.action: Go through the four cards.
instructions.teacher_tip: The answer depends on how much human creative input was involved. Spend your time on "The test".

instructions.action: Leave the two definitions up for pupils to copy.
Go through the three ways, then ask pupils to name one project where they would use AI as a starting point, not a shortcut.
Read the takeaway, then stop.
Say, out loud, who pupils can go to if anything today affected them, and leave the support slides up as the room moves on.
instructions.teacher_tip: Name the actual person — tutor, head of year or safeguarding lead — rather than leaving it to the slide.

title: The hidden costs of AI
preparation: Open the PDF (or the SlideForge deck) on the board before the class arrives.
Optional: have one short article or graphic ready about AI energy use or data centres.

instructions.action: Have the title up and introduce the idea that AI has hidden environmental costs.
instructions.teacher_tip: Keep the tone curious rather than alarming.

instructions.action: Ask the question, give pairs 60 seconds, then ask pupils to place themselves from 1 (not at all) to 5 (enormously).
instructions.teacher_tip: Listen for students who assume online activity is "free" for the planet. Redirect guilt to "when is it worth it?".

instructions.action: Go through the four layers: everything under one chatbot answer.
instructions.teacher_tip: The water layer is the one students remember, because nobody expects computing to be thirsty.

instructions.action: Go through the four cards.
instructions.teacher_tip: Say card B clearly: nobody should leave thinking they have been told off for using a chatbot.

instructions.action: Ask the room which of the five uses is in the wrong place.
instructions.teacher_tip: The positions are arguable, and that is the exercise. Do not defend the exact spots.

instructions.action: Leave the two definitions up for pupils to copy.
Go through the three habits.
instructions.teacher_tip: Keep it balanced: the goal is thoughtful use, not fear of AI.

instructions.action: Read the takeaway, then stop.
Say, out loud, who pupils can go to if anything today affected them, and leave the support slides up as the room moves on.
instructions.teacher_tip: Name the actual person — tutor, head of year or safeguarding lead — rather than leaving it to the slide.

title: Your AI-ready future
preparation: Open the PDF (or the SlideForge deck) on the board before the class arrives.
Optional: have the WEF Future of Jobs Report 2025 figures to hand in case students ask.

instructions.action: Have the title up and introduce the idea that AI is changing careers and work.
instructions.teacher_tip: Set a positive tone: this is about opportunity, not fear.

instructions.action: Ask the question and give pairs 60 seconds. Collect one skill from each pair.
instructions.teacher_tip: Listen for students who focus only on job loss, and draw out the opportunities too.

instructions.action: Read the three figures, leading with the net number.
instructions.teacher_tip: Pause after each figure. "Transformed, not disappeared": most jobs will change rather than vanish.

instructions.action: Go through the four cards, matching them to the skills pairs suggested.
instructions.teacher_tip: "Somebody said kindness — that is this one" makes the list theirs rather than yours.

instructions.action: Leave the two definitions up for pupils to copy.
Go through the three moves and invite pupils to name one habit they will try.
instructions.teacher_tip: End on an empowering note.

instructions.action: Read the takeaway, then stop.
Say, out loud, who pupils can go to if anything today affected them, and leave the support slides up as the room moves on.
instructions.teacher_tip: Name the actual person — tutor, head of year or safeguarding lead — rather than leaving it to the slide.

title: AI is already here!
preparation: Open the PDF (or the SlideForge deck) and check the BBC Ideas film plays with sound in the hall: youtube.com/watch?v=E4bvQZRC6Bo
Have the video open in a browser tab, so you can switch to it on slide 5.
Optional: prepare one live AI prompt and one fact-check example to show.

instructions.action: Have the title up as students come in.
Hook: ask for a show of hands — has anyone used AI today? Then ask whether AI "understands" what it writes.
instructions.teacher_tip: Most hands stay down at first. The next slide changes that.

instructions.action: Go through the four everyday uses, then ask again who has used AI today.
instructions.teacher_tip: Card C is the bridge to the film: a chatbot is autocomplete at enormous scale.

instructions.action: Play the BBC Ideas film "How AI actually works".
instructions.teacher_tip: Ask them to listen for one thing the AI does NOT do.

instructions.action: Discuss: AI as pattern prediction — advanced autocomplete — against genuine understanding. Take two or three answers from the hall.
instructions.student_action: Turn to a neighbour, then answers from the hall
instructions.teacher_tip: Row 3 is the surprise: a model has no way of noticing that it does not know.

instructions.action: Explain hallucinations: plausible wording can still be wrong, so verify important facts.
instructions.teacher_tip: If you prepared a fact-check example, show it here.

instructions.action: Present the three Being AI-smart habits and invite responses from the hall.
Exit check: ask students for one safe use of AI and one use that must be fact-checked.
instructions.student_action: Answer as they leave, or tell a tutor

instructions.action: Signpost reporting and support resources, and leave them up as the hall empties.
instructions.teacher_tip: Name the actual person — tutor, head of year or safeguarding lead — rather than leaving it to the slide.
